title: Intake Questions and Updating Patient Information

sections.learningObjectives:
- Ask appropriate and respectful intake questions to gather complete patient information.
- Update patient demographics, insurance, medication, and allergy information accurately.
- Verify patient information using reliable techniques to prevent identity and data-entry errors.
- Document patient updates correctly and objectively following legal record-keeping standards.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of intake like filling out a name tag and emergency card before an event. It makes sure the right person gets the right care, with the right details written down.

### Question 2

If two kids in a class are both named Jordan, you check their last name and birthday to tell them apart. Clinics do the same thing so the right record goes to the right person.

### Question 3

Demographics are the 'name tag' facts about a person: where they live, how to reach them, and who to call in an emergency.

### Question 4

It is like the 'in case of emergency' name on a permission slip. If something goes wrong, the office knows exactly who to call.

### Question 5

If someone says 'my tummy hurts,' you write 'my tummy hurts,' not a big medical word you made up. Write what they said so the doctor knows exactly what happened.

### Question 6

Open-ended questions are like asking 'tell me about your day' instead of 'did you have a good day?' — they let people give more detail.

### Question 7

Closed questions are like true-or-false checks. They are great for double-checking a birthday or phone number quickly.

### Question 8

If a friend starts talking about their cat when you asked about their homework, you kindly steer back to the homework. The assistant does the same, politely, to get the info needed.

### Question 9

If a friend says their back hurts, you would ask 'where exactly?' and 'since when?' Those details help the doctor understand the problem.

### Question 10

Like checking all the ingredients before baking, listing every medicine helps avoid a bad mix that could make someone sick.

### Question 11

People often forget that vitamins and cough syrup are 'medicines' too. Asking about them specifically catches things a patient might not mention.

### Question 12

Allergies are things a person's body reacts badly to, like peanuts, penicillin, or latex gloves. Asking about all of them keeps the person safe.

### Question 13

If a friend says they are allergic to peanuts, you ask 'what happens?' — a tummy ache is different from trouble breathing. The assistant asks the same to keep them safe.

### Question 14

The assistant writes down what the patient shares without making a mean face or comment. It is just a fact for the doctor to know, like writing down someone's height.

### Question 15

Some things, like certain illnesses, can run in families the way eye color does. Knowing that helps the doctor watch for those things early.

### Question 16

Knowing what surgery someone had and when is like knowing what repairs a car has had — it helps the doctor understand the patient's health story.

### Question 17

The pharmacy is like the mailbox where the doctor's medicine order gets delivered. Asking which one the patient uses makes sure it goes to the right mailbox.

### Question 18

If someone speaks another language, you get a helper who speaks both languages so nothing is missed — you do not just talk louder or guess.

### Question 19

If someone has trouble hearing, you look at them and speak clearly so they can see your face, and you check that they understood.

### Question 20

Some things are private, like a secret. The assistant moves to a quiet room so no one else can overhear the patient's personal health details.

### Question 21

If a friend says 'I just don't feel right,' you would ask 'what feels off?' to understand. The assistant asks a kind follow-up question too.

### Question 22

An advance directive is like a letter a person writes ahead of time about what kind of care they would want. Asking about it helps the office honor those wishes.

### Question 23

People move and change phone numbers all the time. The office checks the 'name tag' details at each visit so the information stays fresh.

### Question 24

Instead of guessing where someone lives, you just ask 'is this still your address?' — quick and accurate.

### Question 25

The office keeps the phone number so it can call or text when it is time for an appointment or when test results are ready.

### Question 26

If someone's name changes, you ask them to spell it so you write it right, then fix it in the system.

### Question 27

A birthday is one of the ways the office tells two people apart. If it is wrong, the office might mix up two people's information.

### Question 28

If the 'call in case of emergency' person changes, the office writes down the new person right away so it is ready when needed.

### Question 29

When someone gets a new job, their insurance often changes too, like switching to a new plan. The office asks so the billing is correct.

### Question 30

After typing, show the person what you wrote and ask 'does this look right?' — that catches little mistakes before they become big ones.

### Question 31

If two classmates have the same name, you check their birthdays to know which is which. The office does the same before changing any information.

### Question 32

Kids usually come with a grown-up who makes decisions for them. The office writes down that grown-up's name and number.

### Question 33

If someone likes to be called 'Sam' instead of 'Samantha,' you call them Sam but still keep their official name on the important forms.

### Question 34

It is like asking someone how they describe themselves instead of guessing — everyone gets to answer for themselves.

### Question 35

Some people like phone calls, some like texts, some like mail. The office asks so it reaches people the way they like best.

### Question 36

If your name is spelled wrong on a form, you would want it fixed. The assistant asks how to spell it correctly and fixes it the right way.

### Question 37

An insurance card is like a two-sided ID. Both sides have important numbers, so you copy both.

### Question 38

It is like checking that a coupon is still valid before using it. The office checks with the insurance company that the plan is active.

### Question 39

If you have two coupons, one is used first and the other helps with what is left. Insurance works the same way: primary first, then secondary.

### Question 40

If a person's insurance changes, the office updates it right away — before sending the bill — so it goes to the right company.

### Question 41

The office makes a clear copy of the card, the way you photocopy a permission slip, and returns the original to the patient.

### Question 42

One wrong digit is like one wrong number in a phone number — the call goes to the wrong place. Fix it to match the card exactly.

### Question 43

COB is like deciding which of two helpers pays first and which one covers the rest, so the bill gets paid without double-charging.

### Question 44

Some plans need a special 'permission slip' before seeing a specialist. The office checks that the slip is in place first.

### Question 45

If someone has no insurance, the office explains the payment options the practice offers, like a lower price or a payment plan, and follows the rules.

### Question 46

If the name on the card and the name on file do not match, the office asks the patient which spelling the insurance company uses, so the bill goes through.

### Question 47

An expired card is like an expired coupon — you do not use it. The office asks for the new one instead.

### Question 48

It is like checking the list of ingredients you wrote down against what is actually in the cupboard, so you notice anything missing or extra.

### Question 49

Writing down a medicine is like writing a recipe step: which ingredient, how much, how often, and how to use it.

### Question 50

If someone cannot remember their medicine names, they can bring the bottles or a list from the pharmacy — like bringing the recipe cards so nothing is forgotten.

### Question 51

The assistant asks, 'anything new, stopped, or different with your medicines?' — a simple check to keep the list up to date.

### Question 52

It is like 'Tylenol' and 'acetaminophen' — two names for the same medicine, the way 'pop' and 'soda' are two names for the same drink.

### Question 53

The list shows what the person actually takes right now, not just what a note said — like a 'what's really in the fridge' list, not an old shopping list.

### Question 54

It is like writing down not just the answer but also who gave it, so the doctor knows where the information came from.

### Question 55

Medicines from different doctors can mix badly, like two things that react in a science experiment. That is why every medicine, from every doctor, goes on one list.

### Question 56

Changing medicine is like adjusting a complicated machine — only the expert doctor decides. The assistant points the patient to the doctor.

### Question 57

A good list is like checking for red flags before a trip — it helps spot problems early, even if it cannot prevent every bump in the road.

### Question 58

Just because you feel better does not mean you should stop a medicine — the doctor needs to be asked first, like asking the captain before changing course.

### Question 59

After a hospital stay, a person often leaves with new medicines. The office adds those to the list so nothing important is missed.

### Question 60

An allergy is when the body's defense system overreacts, while a side effect is just an extra effect the medicine can have — like a medicine making you sleepy.

### Question 61

Writing 'no known allergies' is like checking a box that says 'asked and answered.' A blank box leaves everyone wondering if the question was skipped.

### Question 62

The office asks 'are these still your allergies, and is there anything new?' — a quick check every visit to stay safe.

### Question 63

A new allergy is like a big warning sign — you write it down clearly and tell the doctor right away so nobody uses the thing that is dangerous.

### Question 64

Some people are allergic to latex, which is what many gloves are made of. Knowing this helps the office use different gloves to keep them safe.

### Question 65

Contrast dye is a special liquid used to help take certain pictures inside the body. If someone is allergic, the doctor must know before using it.

### Question 66

Writing 'allergic to X — got a rash' is much more useful than just writing 'allergy.' The details tell the doctor how careful to be.

### Question 67

Allergies go in a special box that sets off an alarm. If you put them in the wrong box, the alarm may not go off, and someone could get hurt.

### Question 68

It is like repeating a phone number back before hanging up, so you know you got every digit right.

### Question 69

Before hitting 'save,' double-check you have the right person's file and the right new information — like checking the address before mailing a letter.

### Question 70

If a name is tricky, ask them to spell it and say it back, just like spelling your name out loud when someone writes it down.

### Question 71

It is like asking someone to tell you their birthday instead of saying 'is it May 1st?' — so they give the real answer, not just a yes.

### Question 72

Numbers get jumbled easily, so you say them back one at a time — like reading a locker combination slowly to double-check it.

### Question 73

If you are not sure something is still true, ask the person instead of guessing — it is the only way to know for sure.

### Question 74

If what a person says does not match what is on the screen, you ask which one is right and fix it — like checking a map when two directions disagree.

### Question 75

Active listening is like really paying attention when a friend tells a story, so you can retell it correctly later.

### Question 76

The assistant writes down the facts without making the patient feel bad — like recording someone's shoe size, no opinions attached.

### Question 77

If someone does not understand a big word, you explain it in simple words — like saying 'tummy' instead of 'abdomen.'

### Question 78

If a friend is upset, you give them a moment and speak kindly. The assistant does the same, so the patient feels safe sharing.

### Question 79

Patient information is a secret that should not be told in a room full of people. If someone starts telling it, the assistant helps move the talk to a private spot.

### Question 80

People have different customs, and the kind thing is to ask questions politely and listen when someone asks for something to be done a certain way.

### Question 81

If you make a mistake in an important notebook, you put one neat line through it and fix it, so everyone can still see what happened — you never rip the page out.

### Question 82

In the computer system, fixing a mistake is done the special way that keeps a record of what was changed and when — you do not just hit delete.

### Question 83

Writing something down right away is like jotting a note before you forget it — do it while it is fresh in your mind.

### Question 84

Write down only what really happened or what the person actually said — the truth, not guesses or opinions.

### Question 85

Saying 'the patient has knee pain' is a fact; saying 'the patient is annoying' is just an opinion. Medical records should only have facts.
